summary: This unit teaches you to understand and use emotional intelligence (EI) as a manager in a public body or other workplace. You will learn the five parts of EI, how to assess your own strengths and limits, how to manage your emotions under pressure, how to read other people's feelings accurately, and how to use these skills in feedback, conflict, customer service and change. You will also learn how to support stressed staff within sensible boundaries and how to plan your own development.

blocks.p: This unit is part of the Business Administration (Management) Level 5 qualification. **Emotional intelligence (EI)** is the ability to recognise and manage your own emotions and to recognise, understand and influence the emotions of other people. Managers in ministries, agencies, municipal corporations, hospitals, schools and businesses meet pressure, conflict, anxious staff and angry members of the public every week. EI does not replace technical knowledge, but it decides how well that knowledge is used.
EI is a set of skills, not a fixed trait. You can measure it, practise it and improve it. It is also a tool for good work with people. It is never a tool for manipulating them.

What this means at work
rows: Explain EI and why it matters
Describe the five parts of EI and how emotions affect decisions, teams and service.
Assess yourself
Use feedback, reflection and tools to find your emotional strengths, triggers and limits.
Manage your own emotions
Pause, name the feeling, choose a response, handle stress and recover from setbacks.
Read other people
Listen actively, notice body language, show empathy and avoid misreading people.
Handle relationships
Give feedback, build trust, resolve conflict, calm angry customers and lead staff through change.
Support staff within limits

Develop EI in yourself and your team
Write a development plan with goals, actions, support and review dates, and build a team climate of trust.

Keep confidences, respect privacy and never use emotional skill to pressure or deceive.

ul: A **multiple-choice theory paper** with workplace scenarios on self-awareness, self-management, empathy, conflict, stress and ethics.
A **written paper** with short answers (exact terms, a short calculation) and longer answers on handling situations in a public office.

**Practical group tasks**: an EI self-assessment with a structured peer-feedback exercise and a personal development plan; and role plays (an angry member of the public, difficult feedback, a conflict between colleagues) with a short counter guide.

blocks.note: Short-answer questions ask for exact terms: EI, Goleman, body language, amygdala hijack, rapport, 360-degree feedback, mindfulness, sympathy, stressor, assertiveness, emotional labour, Johari window, psychological safety and adaptability. Learn them from the key terms in the Revision section.

sections.title: What emotional intelligence is and why it matters

blocks.p: Emotions are quick physical and mental reactions to events: anger, fear, pride, sadness, joy. They are not good or bad in themselves. They give information (this matters to me, something is wrong) and they push us to act. The problem is not having an emotion. The problem is letting it make decisions for us without thinking.
Emotions also **spread**. A manager who arrives each morning tense and irritated passes the mood to the team. A manager who stays calm in a crisis helps others to do the same.

blocks.h: Goleman's model: the five parts of EI

blocks.p: **Daniel Goleman** made emotional intelligence widely known in the 1990s with a five-part model. It is the model the Level 5 programme uses.

head: Part
What it means
Workplace example in a public office
rows: **Self-awareness**
Knowing your own emotions, strengths, limits, values and how you affect others
A supervisor notices that she gets short-tempered late on Fridays and plans her hardest meetings for the morning.
**Self-regulation** (self-management)
Managing your emotions and impulses; staying calm, honest and flexible
A manager criticised in a meeting pauses, breathes and asks what the concern is, instead of snapping back.
**Motivation**
Driving yourself towards goals for their own sake; optimism and resilience
A team whose proposal was turned down by the board studies the feedback and applies again.
**Empathy**
Understanding how others feel and why, and responding with care
A supervisor sees that a cheerful clerk has become withdrawn and asks quietly if she is all right.
**Social skills**
Building relationships, communicating clearly, influencing, managing conflict, working in teams
A manager brings two quarrelling officers together and helps them agree a way forward.

blocks.p: The first three are about **you**; the last two are about **your dealings with other people**. Each part depends on the one before: you cannot read others well until you can read yourself.

blocks.h: Why EI matters for a manager

ul: **Trust:** people follow managers who listen, stay calm and treat them fairly.
**Conflict:** a manager with EI de-escalates arguments before they damage the team.
**Decisions:** strong feelings can bias judgement, so a manager who manages them decides better.
**Service:** staff who manage their emotions deal better with frustrated customers.
**Wellbeing and performance:** teams with a supportive manager have less stress, less absence and better results.
**Change:** managers who understand fear and loss lead people through restructuring and mergers more successfully.

blocks.note: EI does not mean being soft, being nice all the time or avoiding hard decisions. A manager with EI can say no, give bad news and discipline staff, and does it in a way that is firm, fair and respectful.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: Strong emotions narrow our thinking. Anger makes us see threats and want to win; fear makes us avoid risk or avoid the issue; excitement makes us ignore dangers. **Unchecked, emotions can bias judgement.** Before an important decision, such as whether to discipline an officer, ask: how am I feeling? Is that affecting what I see? Should I wait until I am calmer and have checked the facts and the procedure?

Goleman used the term **amygdala hijack** for a sudden, overwhelming emotional reaction. When we feel seriously threatened, the part of the brain that detects danger can take over before the thinking part has had time to work. The result is a flash of anger or panic, a harsh email, a shouted remark, followed by regret. Recognising an early warning (a hot face, fast heart, clenched jaw) lets you stop before the hijack.

People show emotions in different ways. In some cultures people speak loudly and use big gestures when they are interested; in others the same behaviour would seem aggressive. In a team that includes colleagues from several countries, a manager should not assume that quietness means agreement, or loud talk means anger. Ask and check before you judge.

head: Point
Sympathy
Empathy
rows: Meaning
Feeling sorry **for** someone
Understanding how someone feels from **their** point of view
Typical words
"Poor you, that's terrible."
"That sounds really hard. What is the worst part for you?"
Effect
May leave the person feeling pitied or talked down to
Helps the person feel heard and ready to find a way forward

blocks.p: **Emotional labour** is the effort of managing your feelings to meet the demands of a job: staying calm with an angry customer at a counter, staying cheerful when you are tired. It is real work and it is tiring. Managers should recognise it, share the load and give counter staff support and breaks.
Self-awareness is where EI starts. A manager who does not know her own habits cannot change them.

head: Method
How it helps
Limits
rows: **Pause and name the feeling**
Saying to yourself "I feel frustrated" or "I feel anxious" makes the feeling clearer and helps you think before you react
Needs practice; at first you may notice only after you have reacted
**Reflective journal**
A few lines after a difficult event: what happened, what I felt, what I did, what I would do differently. Over weeks it shows **patterns** in your reactions
Only as honest as you are
**360-degree feedback**
Feedback gathered together from your manager, peers and staff gives the most **balanced** view of how your behaviour affects others
Needs a safe, confidential process; raters may be cautious
**Self-assessment tools and tests**
A questionnaire can show strengths and gaps and start a discussion
One view only: check it against what others tell you; a high score does not prove high EI
**Mentor or coach**
Someone who knows you well can reflect your behaviour back
Needs trust and time
**Mindfulness**
Paying calm, full attention to the present moment builds the habit of noticing feelings as they happen
Needs regular practice

blocks.p: A **trigger** is a cue that sets off a strong reaction. It may be a tone of voice, being interrupted, criticism in public, a missed deadline, unfairness or being ignored. Triggers come from past experience. When you know yours, you can see them coming, avoid them where you can, and plan a calmer response when you cannot.
The **Johari window** is a simple model of four "panes" that show what is known and not known about you, to yourself and to other people.

head: Pane
Known to you
Known to others
What to do
rows: **Open**
Yes
Yes
Use it: this is where trust is built
**Blind spot**
No
Yes
Ask for feedback: others see things about you that you do not
**Hidden**
Yes
No
Share suitable things to build trust; keep private what should stay private
**Unknown**
No
No
Learn through new experience and reflection

blocks.p: Feedback shrinks your blind spot. Thoughtful self-disclosure enlarges the open pane.

A manager should know where she is strong (for example, calm in a crisis, good at listening) and where she is limited (for example, avoids conflict, gets impatient with slow work). Knowing your strengths and limits lets you **plan** your work (put difficult conversations in your best time of day), **seek support** (ask a colleague to check your draft when you are angry) and be realistic about what you can take on.

flow: Listen without interrupting or defending yourself
Thank the person: feedback is a gift even when it is uncomfortable
Ask for specific examples: "Which part was unclear? What would you have liked me to do?"
Reflect: is there truth in it? What is the pattern?
Decide what you will change and tell the person you will try

blocks.p: For example, if a director tells you that your presentation was poorly organised, the emotionally intelligent response is to thank her, ask for specifics and reflect, rather than make excuses.

blocks.note: Do not treat one test or one person's comment as the whole truth. Combine your own reflection with feedback from several people.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.h: Managing an emotion is not suppressing it

blocks.p: **Suppressing** an emotion means pushing it down and pretending it is not there. It tends to come out later in worse ways, or damages health. **Managing** an emotion means noticing it, accepting it, and **choosing how to express it**: when, to whom and in what way.

flow: **Notice** the body signals: hot face, tight chest, fast heart, clenched fists
**Pause**: stop talking, breathe slowly (in for four, out for six), count to ten, or step out of the room for a minute
**Name** the feeling to yourself: "I am angry because my work was criticised in front of everyone"
**Ask** what you want to achieve and what the facts are
**Choose** a response that serves that aim: ask a question, state your view calmly, ask for time
**Review** later: what worked and what would you change?

blocks.p: Suppose a councillor criticises Andre's report in front of the whole meeting and he feels angry. The best first response is to pause, breathe and ask what concerns the councillor, not to defend himself loudly or to say nothing and sulk.

head: Strategy
Example
rows: Plan and prioritise
Before a budget deadline, list tasks by urgency and importance; drop or delegate the rest
Short breaks and rest
Five minutes away from the desk, a walk, water, a proper lunch, enough sleep
Healthy outlets
Exercise, time with family and friends, church or community activity, hobbies, music
Ask for help
Share the workload; talk to a trusted colleague, mentor or the employee assistance programme
Cool-off before reacting
If you receive an unfair email late at night and write an angry reply, **save it as a draft and reread it tomorrow**
Wait before deciding
If you are very upset after a heated meeting, do not decide about disciplining someone until you are calm and have checked the procedure
Reframe
Ask: what can I control here? What can I learn from it?

blocks.note: Alcohol, overworking and venting at colleagues are not healthy ways to manage stress. They make the problem worse. If stress continues for weeks, see a doctor or counsellor.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: A **stressor** is a situation or event that causes stress, such as a heavy workload, a threatening customer or fear of job loss. Short bursts of stress can sharpen performance. Long, unrelieved stress leads to **burnout**.

head: Warning sign
Examples
rows: Physical
Constant tiredness, headaches, poor sleep, frequent illness
Emotional
Cynicism, irritability, feeling hopeless or overwhelmed, loss of interest
Behaviour
Withdrawal, missed deadlines, more mistakes, arriving late, working very long hours

blocks.p: **Self-motivation** means pursuing goals for their own value, not only for pay or praise: curiosity, pride in service, a wish to improve. **Resilience** is the ability to recover from setbacks. A resilient manager learns from the board's rejection of a proposal and tries again. Habits that build resilience include setting small goals, celebrating progress, keeping perspective, using support networks and keeping an optimistic but realistic view.

**Adaptability** (flexibility) is adjusting calmly and quickly to new situations and changes: a new system, a new minister, a reorganisation. Managers who adapt keep the team steady; managers who resist create anxiety.

blocks.note: Work in Jamaica's public service often comes with pressure that managers do not control: budgets set late, hurricane-season emergencies, heavy public demand and limited staff. EI does not remove these pressures, but it helps you to stay steady, to protect your team and to ask clearly for what you need.
blocks.label: Jamaica

sections.title: Empathy and social awareness: reading other people

blocks.p: Active listening means giving your full attention and showing that you have understood. It is the most important empathy skill.

ul: Face the person, put away the phone, and keep your body open.
Let the person finish; do not interrupt or prepare your answer while they are speaking.
Show interest with a nod, eye contact (as is comfortable and appropriate in the culture) and short responses such as "I see".
Ask open questions: "What happened next?" "How did that affect you?"
**Summarise and check:** "So you are saying that the new procedure doubled your workload, and no one told you in advance. Is that right?"
Notice what is not said: pauses, tone and body language.

blocks.p: **Body language** is the set of messages people send through posture, gestures, facial expression and eye contact. Tone of voice adds to it. When what is said does not match the body language, notice the mismatch, but do not jump to conclusions.

head: Signal
Could mean
But check, because it could also mean
rows: Arms crossed, frowning
Closed to what is said, or disagreeing
Feeling cold, concentrating, or a habit
Little eye contact
Discomfort, shyness, or dishonesty
Respect in some cultures; tiredness
Quiet and withdrawn
Sad, worried, angry
Thinking, or simply an introvert
Loud voice, fast speech
Anger or excitement
A natural speaking style

blocks.note: Your own body language sends messages as well. If you sit with arms crossed and frown while staff speak in a tense meeting, they may read this as a sign that you are closed to their views. Check your posture, face and tone.
blocks.label: Tip

ul: Treat what you see as a **hypothesis** and check it: "You seem quiet today. Is everything all right?"
Compare with how the person normally behaves: a **change** from normal is a more reliable signal than a single behaviour.
Allow for cultural and personal style.
Do not label ("she is difficult") or assume you know the reason.
Listen for the facts and the feeling behind them.

blocks.h: Noticing a change in a team member

blocks.p: A usually cheerful records clerk has been quiet, avoiding eye contact and eating lunch alone for a week. Her supervisor should talk to her **privately**, say what she has noticed, and ask how she is. She should listen without pressing, respect the answer, and offer practical help.

**Rapport** is a relationship of mutual understanding and trust. Build it by showing real interest in people and their work, remembering what matters to them, being consistent, doing what you say you will do and being honest.

EI also includes reading the **organisation**: who has influence, how key people feel about a proposed change, which relationships matter. Before proposing a sensitive change at a statutory body, a manager who finds out who has influence and how key people feel is using **social awareness**. It is not manipulation: it is preparation, so that the change is explained well and concerns are heard.

head: Do
Do not
rows: Offer to talk and let the person decide how much to say
Press for private details
Keep what you hear confidential, within the limits of safety and policy
Share it with other staff or gossip
Offer practical support (adjusted workload, leave, referral)
Try to counsel or diagnose a serious problem yourself
Refer to professional help when needed
Promise to keep a secret if someone may be in danger

blocks.note: A manager is not a doctor or a counsellor. If a staff member says she has felt hopeless for weeks and cannot sleep, listen, take it seriously, and help her to reach professional support: her doctor, the employee assistance programme or another service the employer provides. If you think she may harm herself or anyone else, get help at once and follow your organisation's emergency procedure.
blocks.label: Safety

sections.title: Relationships: feedback, conflict, customers and change

flow: Choose a **private** place and a calm time, and prepare your facts
State the purpose and put the person at ease
Describe the **specific behaviour** and its effect with facts and examples, not labels
Listen to the person's view and ask questions
Agree what will change, what support you will give and when you will check
End on a clear, respectful note

blocks.p: Suppose Karen must tell a long-serving officer that his reports have repeated errors. The most emotionally intelligent approach is to speak privately, give the facts, listen to him and agree a way forward, rather than criticising him in front of others, sending an email, or saying nothing.

head: Weak
Better
rows: "You're always careless."
"In the last four reports I found six figures that did not match the source data. What is getting in the way, and how can I help?"
"Good work, everyone."
"Marcia, the way you explained the new form to the public yesterday was clear and patient. It saved the counter a lot of time."

blocks.p: The most effective praise is **specific and timely**. Say what was done, what difference it made and thank the person soon after. General praise sounds empty, and late praise loses its effect.

flow: **Calm things first**: if two officers argue loudly, separate them or take the discussion out of public view
**Hear each person privately**: let each tell the story, reflect the feelings and the facts, and do not take sides
**Find the shared interest**: both want the work done and a decent working relationship
**Bring them together** when they are calm: each states the problem without blaming; agree what each will do
**Agree specific actions and a follow-up date**, and check back
**Escalate or refer** (HR, mediation) if it continues or becomes harassment or bullying

blocks.note: If a team is taking sides after a quarrel between two senior officers, do not let it go on. Speak to each person privately, then together, and make it clear that the team's work and respect for one another come first.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: **Assertiveness** means stating your needs and views clearly and respectfully, without being passive (letting others override you) or aggressive (overriding others).

head: Style
What it sounds like
rows: Passive
"Oh, it's fine, I'll just do it myself again."
Aggressive
"You never do your share. This is useless."
Assertive
"I have done the last three reports. I need us to share them, starting with this one. Can you take it?"

blocks.h: Handling an angry member of the public

blocks.p: Counter staff in a tax office, a passport office or a municipal corporation face frustrated people every day. A person who shouts about a long wait is usually angry about the delay, not about you.

flow: **Stay calm** and keep your voice low and slow; do not take it personally
**Listen** without interrupting while the person lets off steam
**Acknowledge the feeling**: "I understand that you have waited a long time, and I would be frustrated too"
**Apologise for the inconvenience** where fitting, without blaming others
**Move to solutions**: explain what can be done, give a realistic time, and write down what you will do
**Know your limits**: call a supervisor if the person is abusive or threatens you, and follow the office's safety procedure
**Recover afterwards**: take a short break, talk with a colleague if needed, and note the incident

blocks.note: Staff are not required to take threats or abuse. If a person threatens violence, step back, call a supervisor or security, and follow the office's safety procedure.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.h: Building trust with a new team

blocks.p: A new manager joining a municipal corporation office where staff distrust management should begin by **meeting staff and listening to them**: one-to-one conversations, asking what works and what does not, and doing something visible about what she hears. Trust grows from showing genuine interest in people's work and keeping promises.

A team has **psychological safety** when people feel safe to speak up, admit mistakes and try new ideas without fear of ridicule or punishment. A manager builds it by thanking people for raising problems, admitting her own mistakes, and responding to bad news calmly. To develop EI as a team:

ul: review hard moments together after the event: what happened, how we felt, what we learned;
invite every member's view in turn, so that quiet officers are heard and the loudest do not dominate;
agree team rules for respectful disagreement;
share workloads fairly, so that one officer is not always left to finish tasks others have passed on.

blocks.p: In a merger of two departments or a restructuring of a statutory body, staff are anxious about their jobs. A manager with EI will:

ul: **Share what she can**, honestly and early, and say clearly what is not yet known;
**Hear concerns** in meetings and one-to-ones, and respond to them;
acknowledge that feelings of loss and fear are normal;
give staff a role in shaping how the change is carried out;
keep to what she promises; do not make promises she cannot keep;
watch for stress and offer support.

sections.title: Ethics, limits and your development plan

blocks.p: EI skills can be used to help people or to control them. A manager who uses her skill at reading people to pressure a junior officer into approving something against the rules is **manipulating**, not showing EI. Real EI respects the other person's interests, honesty and dignity.

head: Ethical use
Manipulation
rows: Understand feelings so as to help and to decide better
Exploit fear, guilt or loyalty to get your own way
Persuade with honest reasons
Pressure someone to break rules or ignore their own judgement
Keep private information private
Use what you learn about a person's weak points against them

blocks.p: EI can be one factor in recruitment. A good interview question asks for evidence of past behaviour, for example: "How did you handle a recent conflict with a colleague?" Look for the candidate's awareness of her own role, her listening and the outcome. It should be used together with skills and qualifications and applied fairly to every candidate.
A plan is only useful if it is specific and followed up. It should have **a goal, actions, support and a review date**.

head: Part
Example
rows: Strength to keep
Calm with the public at the counter
Area to develop
Reacting sharply to criticism in meetings
Goal
For the next six months, pause and ask a question before responding to any criticism in meetings
Actions
Keep a reflective journal; practise the pause-and-choose routine; read a short book on assertiveness; attend a workshop
Support
Ask my mentor to give feedback after two meetings a month; use the employee assistance programme if I need it
Measure
Feedback from three colleagues at the review; fewer incidents noted in the journal
Review date
Check progress in three months and adjust

blocks.p: To keep improving over time, **seek feedback and reflect regularly**. EI grows with practice, not with one course.

Suppose a team leader often loses his temper with the public at a service counter. His manager can help him best by coaching him to spot his triggers and plan how he will respond, rather than by threatening him, ignoring it or moving him to the back office at once. Agree goals, practise with role play, give feedback and review.

blocks.note: Team members' EI scores and personal feedback are confidential. Do not display or discuss them with others without permission, and use them only to help development, never to label people.
blocks.label: Remember

ul: define emotional intelligence and name the five parts in Goleman's model.

terms: Emotional intelligence (EI)
The ability to recognise and manage your own emotions and to understand and influence those of others
Self-awareness
Knowing your own emotions, strengths, limits and effect on others
Self-regulation
Managing your emotions and impulses, and choosing how to respond

Body language

Rapport

Paying calm, full attention to the present moment

The effort of managing feelings to meet the demands of a job

Employee assistance programme (EAP)
A confidential support service that an employer provides to staff
Burnout

c1.title: A tense budget season at a ministry in Kingston
c1.text: Natalie Francis is a director at a ministry in Kingston. The budget deadline is in six days and her team of nine is working late. She has noticed that she snaps at staff in the afternoons and that last week she sent an angry email at 11 p.m. to an officer in another department, which she regrets. A colleague has told her, kindly, that she sometimes sits with her arms folded and frowns during team meetings, and that people stop speaking when she does so.

c2.title: The counter at a parish revenue office in St Ann
c2.text: Kevin Dixon works at the counter of a municipal corporation revenue office in St Ann's Bay. A man whose property tax receipt has been delayed for three weeks comes in at 2 p.m. after waiting 45 minutes in the queue. He raises his voice, says that "nobody in this place does any work", and points at the clerks. The supervisor, Ms Hylton, is in the office. There are ten other people waiting and the system is slow.

c3.title: A withdrawn clerk in a health records office
c3.text: Shelly-Ann is a records clerk at a regional health authority in Montego Bay. For two weeks she has been quiet and tearful, has made more errors than usual and has stopped joining her colleagues for lunch. Her supervisor, Mr Gordon, knows that she is normally cheerful and reliable. Yesterday she told him, briefly, that she had not been sleeping and had felt hopeless for some time.

c4.title: Two senior officers who stopped speaking
c4.text: At a statutory body in Spanish Town, two senior officers, Mr Campbell and Mrs Lawrence, disagreed in a meeting about who should lead a joint project. Since then they communicate only by email and the team has begun to take sides: some staff avoid one or the other, and meetings have become tense. The head of the division, Dr Samuels, has to resolve the situation. Meanwhile the statutory body is also preparing to merge with another agency, and staff are anxious about their posts.

c5.title: An EI development plan for a new manager
c5.text: Trevor Walker has just been promoted to manager of a team of twelve at a municipal corporation in Portmore. His 360-degree feedback shows that staff rate him high on knowing his job but low on listening and on staying calm when work goes wrong. His own self-assessment questionnaire gave him a high EI score. Trevor wants to use his results well.

questions.q: Natalie notices that she snaps at people most afternoons. Which part of EI is she using when she notices this pattern?
o: Self-regulation, because she is already controlling the way she behaves
Empathy, because she is thinking about how her staff feel
Self-awareness, because she is recognising her own emotional habits
Motivation, because she is working to meet her deadline
questions.why: Self-awareness is knowing your own emotions and how they show. Noticing the pattern comes before managing it, which is self-regulation.

questions.q: It is 11 p.m. and Natalie has just read an unfair email from another department. She has typed an angry reply. What should she do?
o: Save the reply as a draft, and reread it and decide the next morning
Send it now, so that the other department understands how serious the matter is
Delete the reply and never answer the email, so that the matter is closed
Send it, then follow up with an apology the next day if it seems too harsh
questions.why: A cooling-off period lets the emotion settle and lets her answer with the facts. Sending an angry message cannot be undone.

questions.q: What message are Natalie's staff most likely to take from her folded arms and frown during meetings?
o: That she agrees with the views being put forward
That she is feeling cold in the air-conditioned room
That she is thinking about the budget and not about them
That she is closed to what they are saying
questions.why: Body language carries messages. Even if she does not intend it, staff are likely to read crossed arms and a frown as a sign that she is closed or disapproving, so she should check her posture and expression.

questions.q: Which step would give Natalie the most balanced picture of how her behaviour affects her team?
o: Taking an online self-test about emotional intelligence and reading her score
Collecting feedback from staff, peers and her own manager at the same time
Asking her deputy, who is also her close friend, to give her an honest opinion
Writing down what she believes the staff think of her management style
questions.why: 360-degree feedback combines several views and shows blind spots. A self-test or one friendly opinion is only one view.

questions.q: What should Kevin do first with the angry man?
o: Explain that the system is slow, and the delay is not the fault of the staff
Stay calm, let him speak and acknowledge that he has waited a long time
Tell him that shouting is not allowed and that he must leave if he continues
Ask the other customers to step back so that no one hears the discussion
questions.why: Listening and acknowledging the feeling usually lowers the temperature. Explaining or warning at once can feel like a dismissal and raise the anger.

questions.q: The man says he has waited too long. Which response shows the most EI?
o: "I know exactly how you feel. Everybody has to wait here, and today is no different from any other day."
"Sir, please lower your voice, because I cannot help you while you are shouting at my colleagues here."
"I am sorry, but this is a Ministry of Finance problem and there is nothing that we can do about it here."
"I understand that three weeks is a long wait, and I would be frustrated too. Let me see what I can do."
questions.why: The best reply names the feeling, shows understanding and moves to a solution. The others dismiss his experience, issue an order or shift the blame.

questions.q: The man continues and then threatens to hit a clerk. What should Kevin do?
o: Step back, call Ms Hylton or security and follow the office safety procedure
Stay at the counter and keep calm, as that is the job of customer service staff
Match the man's voice so that he knows that Kevin will not be intimidated
Offer him a quick decision on his receipt so that he leaves as soon as possible
questions.why: Staff need not accept threats of violence. Calm manner is for abuse and frustration; a threat calls for help and the safety procedure.

questions.q: After the incident Kevin feels shaken and the next customer is waiting. What is the best step for Ms Hylton?
o: Tell Kevin to carry on at once because other customers are waiting
Ask Kevin to write a long report before he returns to the counter
Give Kevin a short break, check how he is, and note the incident
Send Kevin home for the rest of the week without discussing it
questions.why: Serving angry customers is emotional labour and takes a toll. A short break and a check-in help recovery, and noting the incident supports later follow-up.

questions.q: What should Mr Gordon do first about Shelly-Ann?
o: Tell her colleagues, so that they can be extra kind to her at work
Start the poor-performance procedure, because her errors are now frequent enough to count
Wait for another month in case the problem solves itself without any help from work
Speak to her privately, listen and offer help to find support
questions.why: She has described serious distress. A private conversation, listening, and help to reach professional support come before any performance procedure, and it must stay confidential.

questions.q: Shelly-Ann says that she has felt hopeless for a long time. What is the best way for Mr Gordon to respond?
o: Reassure her that every job feels hopeless sometimes and that she will soon feel better
Take it seriously, listen and help her reach her doctor or the employee assistance programme
Offer to counsel her himself, as he knows her well and she clearly trusts him with this
Promise to keep whatever she says secret, whatever she may tell him in the future
questions.why: A manager is not a counsellor. Take her seriously and help her to reach professional help. He cannot promise secrecy if she or anyone else may be in danger.

questions.q: Which of these is a warning sign of burnout that Mr Gordon may be seeing?
o: Rapid improvement in her work when she is given a deadline
A wish to take on new tasks and to lead projects
Withdrawal, more errors and constant tiredness
Frequent requests for praise from her colleagues
questions.why: Burnout shows as exhaustion, cynicism, withdrawal, more mistakes and loss of interest. The other options point the opposite way.

questions.q: What is the best first step for Dr Samuels in the dispute between Mr Campbell and Mrs Lawrence?
o: Meet each of them privately and hear their views, without taking sides
Call a team meeting and ask staff to say who they think is right
Order both of them to make up and report to him when it is done
Remove one of them from the project to stop the disagreement quickly
questions.why: Hearing each person privately lets them talk freely and shows fairness. Public voting, an order or a removal does not deal with the causes.

questions.q: When Dr Samuels brings Mr Campbell and Mrs Lawrence together, which approach is most likely to work?
o: Ask each to state the problem without blaming, find the shared aim and agree specific actions
Ask each to say what the other has done wrong, so that Dr Samuels can judge who is at fault
Ask them to forget the disagreement and to say nothing more about it in the future
Let them argue it out and step in only if the discussion becomes loud
questions.why: Starting from the shared interest in the work, and agreeing actions without blame, moves people forward. Blame or silence tends to leave the cause unsolved.

questions.q: Staff at the statutory body fear for their jobs in the merger. What should Dr Samuels do?
o: Say nothing until every detail of the merger is certain
Promise that nobody will lose a post, so that staff are calm
Share what he can, say what is not yet known and listen to concerns
Tell staff that worry is unprofessional and they should focus on their work
questions.why: Honest sharing of what is known, and of what is not, together with hearing concerns, builds trust in change. False promises or silence harm trust.

questions.q: Which action best builds psychological safety in Dr Samuels' division?
o: Asking staff to put every concern in writing, so that there is a record
Thanking staff who raise problems and admitting his own mistakes
Giving a public reward each month to the officer who makes the fewest mistakes
Holding meetings only with the senior officers and passing on the decisions
questions.why: People speak up when they see that raising problems is welcome and that the leader is open about mistakes.

questions.q: Trevor scored himself high on an EI questionnaire, but his 360-degree feedback is low on listening. How should he treat the results?
o: Trust the questionnaire, because he knows himself better than other people do
Ignore both sets of results, because they cannot be measured accurately
Accept the feedback and conclude that his own score was dishonest
Treat the questionnaire as one view and take the feedback on listening seriously
questions.why: A self-test is only one view and may not match how others see you. Several raters give a better picture, and Trevor should check the gap with them.

questions.q: Which item is essential in Trevor's development plan?
o: A list of his team's weaknesses and the steps he will take to correct them
A specific goal, actions, support and a review date
A promise to be calm at all times and to listen to every complaint made
A copy of his scores displayed in the office so that staff can hold him to them
questions.why: A plan needs a measurable goal, planned actions, support and a date to review progress. His scores and feedback are confidential.

questions.q: Trevor's colleagues say that he often interrupts and raises his voice when work goes wrong, but he is unaware of it. In the Johari window, where does this behaviour sit?
o: In his blind spot: it is known to others but not to him
In his open pane, because everyone knows about it
In his hidden pane, because he is keeping it from others
In his unknown pane, because nobody has noticed it yet
questions.why: A blind spot is something others see about you that you do not. Feedback is the way to shrink it.

questions.q: A cashier at a public hospital stays patient and pleasant with anxious families all day and is exhausted by the evening. Which term best describes the effort she is making?
o: Self-motivation
Rapport building
Adaptability
Emotional labour
questions.why: Emotional labour is the effort of managing feelings to meet the demands of a job. Managers should recognise it, share the load and allow short breaks.

questions.q: A team leader has covered for a colleague who never finishes his share of the filing. She sighs and says, 'Never mind, I will do it myself again.' Which communication style is this?
o: Aggressive, because she is blaming her colleague
Assertive, because she is staying calm and polite
Passive, because she does not state what she needs
Empathic, because she is putting his feelings first
questions.why: A passive style avoids stating a need and lets the problem continue. An assertive style would say clearly what is needed, for example: 'I need us to share the filing, starting today.'
